content: The WHO Steering Group was responsible for overseeing the collection and synthesis of evidence, organizing the Guideline Development Group (GDG) meetings, drafting and finalizing the guideline document, and managing the dissemination, implementation, and impact assessment of the guidelines. The members of the WHO Steering Group are listed in Annex 1. The WHO Steering Group identified a pool of approximately 50 experts and stakeholders from all six WHO regions to form the Maternal and Perinatal Health Guideline Development Group (MPH-GDG). This group included individuals with expertise in critically appraising research evidence, implementing evidence-based recommendations, guideline development methods, clinical practice, policy, and maternal and perinatal health programs. A consumer representative was also included. From this pool, 16 external experts and stakeholders were invited to participate in updating the recommendations, focusing on the prevention and treatment of peripartum infections. These members were selected for their diverse expertise in research, guideline development, gender equity, clinical practice, policy, and consumer representation. The GDG members for this recommendation are listed in Annex 1. The Evidence Synthesis Group (ESG) was convened by WHO and included guideline methodologists and systematic review teams. They conducted or updated systematic reviews, appraised evidence, and developed evidence-to-decision (EtD) frameworks. A systematic review on the effects of the intervention was updated with the support of the Cochrane Pregnancy and Childbirth Group. The WHO Steering Group reviewed and provided input into the updated protocol and worked closely with the Cochrane Group and methodologists to appraise the evidence using the GRADE methodology. Representatives from the Cochrane Group and methodologists attended GDG meetings to present evidence and respond to technical queries. ESG members are listed in Annex 1. Representatives from external organizations, including USAID, the International Confederation of Midwives (ICM), the International Federation of Gynecology and Obstetrics (FIGO), and the Bill & Melinda Gates Foundation, participated in GDG meetings as observers. These organizations, with a history of collaboration with WHO in maternal and perinatal health, were identified as potential implementers of the recommendations. The list of observers is included in Annex 1. The External Review Group (ERG) consisted of eight technical experts with interests and expertise in preventing and treating peripartum infections. This group was geographically diverse, gender-balanced, and free of significant conflicts of interest. The ERG reviewed the final document to identify factual errors, comment on language clarity, and address contextual issues and implementation implications. The ERG did not have the authority to change the recommendations formulated by the GDG. Members of the ERG are listed in Annex 1. The priority outcomes for this guideline update were aligned with those from the 2015 WHO recommendations on preventing and treating maternal peripartum infections. Evidence on these outcomes was included in the scope of this document for evidence retrieval, synthesis, grading, and recommendation formulation. The list of priority outcomes is provided in Annex 2. Evidence to support this update was derived from multiple sources by the ESG in collaboration with the WHO Steering Group. An updated systematic review on prophylactic antibiotics for women undergoing cesarean section served as the primary source of evidence. Four additional studies involving 856 women were included since the previous review. Data from randomized controlled trials were analyzed using Review Manager (RevMan) software and appraised using GRADE criteria. Evidence profiles were prepared for key comparisons and outcomes, including risk assessments. A mixed-methods systematic review provided evidence on values, resource use, cost-effectiveness, equity, acceptability, and feasibility related to prophylactic antibiotics for cesarean sections. This review included the perspectives of women and providers and identified factors influencing antibiotic use during childbirth. The certainty of evidence for each outcome was assessed using the GRADE approach, with ratings of high, moderate, low, or very low based on study design limitations, inconsistency, indirectness, imprecision, and publication bias. Findings from qualitative reviews were appraised using the GRADE-CERQual tool, which assessed confidence in qualitative evidence based on methodological limitations, data adequacy, coherence, and relevance. The WHO Steering Group prepared summary tables and evidence narratives using the GRADE EtD framework. These frameworks systematically considered evidence on effects, values, resources, equity, acceptability, and feasibility to guide decision-making. The GDG reviewed these documents before their meeting and collectively formulated recommendations during the meeting. Decisions were made by consensus, defined as agreement by at least three-quarters of participants, with no opposition expressed. All experts were required to disclose potential conflicts of interest, which were reviewed and managed according to WHO procedures. Summaries of DOI statements and their management are provided in Annex 3. The GDG reviewed evidence summaries and applied additional criteria, including stakeholder values, resource implications, acceptability, feasibility, and equity, to determine the direction and strength of the recommendations. Decisions were based on consensus, and the final document was reviewed and approved by the GDG and ERG. External peer reviewers provided additional input, which was incorporated to correct factual errors and improve clarity. The guiding principles and best practices adopted by the 2020 GDG panel were based on expert consensus and aimed to improve care related to preventing and treating infectious morbidities during childbirth. These principles emphasized good clinical practices, such as providing nutritional advice, addressing maternal medical conditions, ensuring infection control, and maintaining reliable supply systems for essential antibiotics. Antibiotics should only be administered when medically indicated to reduce antimicrobial resistance.
